activities.anchor: the procedure is the same, and it has steps
activities.caption: sequence the passes on an unseen extract
activities.name: crPassesOrder

config.prompt: An unseen extract lands in front of you — order the method:
items: Gist: read once for what happens and who is speaking — no annotating yet
Language: read again slowly, marking everything deliberate
Structure: how the passage moves — where it turns, what is set up and what pays off
Zoom out: the local patterns become the global claim
config.why: You cannot weigh words before you know what the passage is doing — and close reading serves interpretation, never replaces it.

activities.caption: fill the blanks in the worked miniature
activities.name: crDickinsonCloze

config.text: Second pass on “Because I could not stop for Death”: the diction (“%%0%%”) is the shock — Death as a courteous suitor, not horror — and “%%1%%” repeats, first as her refusal, then as his courtesy.
config.hint: One is an ordinary adverb doing the whole poem's work; the other is the word that repeats.

activities.caption: pair each noun with the attitude it signals
activities.name: crNounsMatch

config.prompt: Four nouns for the same young humans — pair each with the attitude it signals:
config.why: The writer's actual choice has what the alternatives lack — and that difference is the effect.

activities.caption: file each word by the layer of the wardrobe it sits in
activities.name: crRegisterBuckets

config.prompt: English keeps a layered wardrobe — file each word:
buckets: Anglo-Saxon short words — close to the body
Latinate longer words — formal or abstract
config.why: A writer who switches layers mid-passage is usually doing something — the collision of the sudden plain word with fancy ones is the meaning.

activities.anchor: images of disease, blood and darkness arrive in waves
activities.caption: guess before you count
activities.name: crSleepEstimate

config.prompt: In Macbeth, critics have counted the mentions of a single word — 'sleep'. Roughly how many times does it occur across the play?
config.why: Over thirty — and nearly always as something murdered, lost or poisoned: Macbeth 'murders sleep' the night he kills Duncan.
config.context: The pattern argues what no single line states: regicide as a sickness infecting the whole body of Scotland.

activities.anchor: That earns almost nothing in an essay
activities.caption: drag the divider — picturing versus arguing
activities.name: crImageCompare

config.prompt: What is an image for? Drag the divider between the dead answer and the live question:

before.label: The dead answer
before.text: Imagery is decoration whose job is to help the reader picture the scene — true of nearly every image ever written, which is why it scores so little.

after.label: The live question
after.text: What does the image cluster argue — which properties travel from vehicle to tenor, and how does the pattern develop?

config.why: The strongest answers treat an image as an argument wearing a picture.

activities.caption: true or false — the sentence is doing something
activities.name: crSyntaxJudge

statements.s: A short sentence arriving after long ones hits with sudden force.
statements.why: Length changes are choices — the shift itself performs the blow.

statements.s: Repeated 'and' suggests piling up; 'although… yet' suggests wrestling.
statements.why: Coordination versus subordination — grammar mimes experience.

statements.s: A sentence's opening word carries special emphasis.
statements.why: Whatever opens the sentence is stressed — see the urgent command that opens 'Never give all the heart'.

statements.s: Opening a sentence with its object instead of its subject is a grammatical accident.
statements.why: In prose it is a small, readable decision worth noting.

activities.caption: you have named the figure — now earn the marks
activities.name: crFigureBranch

config.root: An examiner's question: what does the personification in 'Death kindly stopped' accomplish? Walk the answering decision:

start.text: You have named the figure. What does your next sentence do?

choices.label: Stop there — the name is the answer
choices.feedback: Naming earns almost nothing by itself — the question is what the figure accomplishes.

choices.label: State its job: what it achieves that plain statement could not

name-only.text: 'The poet uses personification.' True, and worth nothing — go back and spend the sentence on the figure's work.

job.text: 'Personifying death as a gentleman caller lets the poem dramatise acceptance instead of terror.' The figure's whole theology, stated — not decoration but the poem's argument in one word.

config.why: Rule of thumb: name the figure, then spend the rest of the sentence on its job.
